title: NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555)
source: Directive (EU) 2022/2555, as published on EUR-Lex; national transposition may add to it
licence: EU law. Titles are the official article headings; purpose, guidance, audit questions and typical evidence are our own words. Read the official text on EUR-Lex.

requirements.title: Article 20 · Governance
requirements.purpose: Puts responsibility for cybersecurity on the leadership of in-scope organisations rather than leaving it to IT alone.

requirements.title: Management approves the measures and oversees them
requirements.purpose: Makes the management body itself approve the cybersecurity risk measures, oversee how they are put in place and accept that its members can be held personally liable when the entity breaches Article 21.
requirements.guidance: The duty sits with the management body, such as the board or managing directors, not with IT or the security lead; they can prepare the material but the decision is management's. Put cybersecurity on the management agenda on a fixed cycle, approve the risk assessment and the measures, and record challenge and decisions in minutes. Give members a short report on risks, incidents, open actions and budget needs. Liability is set by national law: check your transposing act, which may add personal duties or fines. For essential entities, authorities can as a last resort temporarily bar a chief executive or legal representative from managerial functions. Auditors often find policies signed off by IT only and no trace that management ever questioned the results.
questions: Which members of the management body approved the cybersecurity risk measures, and when?
How does the management body oversee implementation between approvals?
What reports does management receive, and what decisions has it taken on them?
How have you checked what your national transposing law says about management liability?
evidence: Management body resolution approving the risk measures, with date
Board or management minutes showing cybersecurity discussion and decisions
Periodic cybersecurity report to the management body
Allocation of cybersecurity responsibilities within the management body
Note on management duties and liability under the national transposing law

requirements.title: Management and staff take cybersecurity training
requirements.purpose: Makes training compulsory for members of the management body so they can recognise cyber risks and judge the security measures and their effect on services, and encourages similar regular training for staff.
requirements.guidance: Treat training of the management body as mandatory: each member, including new appointees, should attend and records should show it. Cover the current threat picture, the entity's own risks, Article 21 measures, incident reporting duties and management's personal accountability, and refresh it regularly. The directive only encourages regular training for other employees, but national law may go further and Article 21(2)(g) already expects awareness training for all staff, so link the two programmes. Auditors find a one-off session years ago, members who never attended and no content records. Keep slides or agendas so the scope can be shown.
questions: When did each member of the management body last complete cybersecurity training?
What did the management training cover, and who delivered it?
How are newly appointed members trained?
How is regular training offered to other employees, and how does it link to your awareness programme?
evidence: Attendance records per management body member with dates
Induction checklist for new board or management members
Staff training offer and completion report

requirements.title: Article 21 · Cybersecurity risk-management measures
requirements.purpose: Sets the baseline set of security measures in-scope organisations must take, proportionate to their risk and size.

requirements.title: Measures that fit the risk
requirements.purpose: Requires technical, operational and organisational measures that match the risks to your systems and the services you provide.
requirements.guidance: Start from a documented risk assessment of the network and information systems you rely on, and of how an incident would affect your customers and other services. Size the measures to your exposure, your size, the likelihood and severity of incidents, the state of the art, relevant standards and the cost. The same measures apply to essential and important entities; what differs is supervision (proactive for essential, after the event for important) and the maximum fines. Digital providers such as cloud, data centre, managed service and DNS providers must also meet the detailed technical rules in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690. Check your national transposing law, which may add requirements. Auditors look for reasoning that links risks to measures, not a copied checklist.
questions: How did you determine that your measures are appropriate and proportionate?
Which risks drove your current security priorities?
Are you an essential or important entity, and how did you confirm that?
Which national law or implementing rules apply to you on top of the directive?
How often is the risk assessment updated?
evidence: Register of measures linked to risks
Entity classification and registration record with the national authority
Mapping to national law or Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 where applicable
Scope statement of systems and services

requirements.title: Risk analysis and security policies for systems
requirements.purpose: Requires you to analyse risks to your information systems and to have policies that set out how they are protected.
requirements.guidance: Keep a policy set covering information security, acceptable use, access, change and data handling, each with an owner and review date. Maintain a risk register with likelihood, impact, owner and treatment decisions. Update it after incidents, major changes or new suppliers. Auditors find policies not matched by practice and risk registers never revisited. Keep documents short enough that staff actually read them.
questions: Where are your security policies and who owns them?
How is the risk register maintained and reviewed?
How do you decide to accept or treat a risk?
How are policies communicated to staff?
evidence: Information security policy set with versions

requirements.title: Handling incidents
requirements.purpose: Requires you to be able to detect, assess, contain and recover from security incidents in an organised way.
requirements.guidance: Define what counts as an incident, how staff report one, who leads response and how severity is judged. Provide logging and monitoring that can actually detect problems. Keep an incident log with timeline, cause, lessons and actions. Link the process to regulatory reporting deadlines. Auditors find no tested procedure, incidents handled informally and lessons never turned into actions. Rehearse, for example with a tabletop exercise, at intervals you set; many entities do so yearly.
questions: How do staff report a suspected incident?
Who decides severity and leads response?
What monitoring detects incidents?
How do you capture and act on lessons learned?

requirements.title: Continuity, backups, disaster recovery and crisis handling
requirements.purpose: Requires plans so that critical services can keep running or be restored after a disruption, with a way to manage a crisis.
requirements.guidance: Identify critical services and set recovery time and data loss targets with the business. Back up key data using separate, protected copies and test restoring regularly. Write recovery and crisis communication plans with named roles and contact lists, and practise them. Auditors often find backups that have never been restored and plans that do not match real dependencies. Include key suppliers in the plan.
questions: Which services are critical and what recovery targets apply?
When did you last restore from backup successfully?
Who runs a crisis and how is communication handled?
How are suppliers covered by the continuity plan?
evidence: Backup schedule and restore test results

requirements.title: Security of the supply chain and direct suppliers
requirements.purpose: Requires you to manage security risks that come from suppliers and service providers.
requirements.guidance: Maintain a register of suppliers with a criticality rating and a named owner. Do proportionate due diligence before onboarding and include security terms in contracts, such as incident notification, access limits and audit rights. Review important suppliers periodically and plan exit routes. Auditors find missing contract terms, no review of existing suppliers and no view of fourth parties. Focus effort on the few suppliers whose failure would hurt most.
questions: Which suppliers are critical and how did you decide that?
What security terms are in supplier contracts?
How do you review supplier security over time?
What happens if a critical supplier fails or is breached?
evidence: Contract clauses on security and incident notice

requirements.title: Secure buying, building and upkeep of systems, with vulnerability handling
requirements.purpose: Requires security to be considered when acquiring and developing systems, and weaknesses to be found and handled.
requirements.guidance: Set security requirements for purchases and new builds, and require review before go-live. Patch on a defined timetable with faster handling for critical flaws, and scan regularly. Track vulnerabilities to closure and accept exceptions formally. If you build or operate software, offer a way for outsiders to report issues and handle disclosures responsibly, in line with your national coordinated disclosure arrangements. Auditors find unpatched systems, scanning that misses parts of the estate and changes without security review.
questions: How are security requirements set when buying or building systems?
What is your patching timeline for critical vulnerabilities?
How do you find vulnerabilities?
How do you handle reports from outside researchers?

requirements.title: Checking whether the measures work
requirements.purpose: Requires you to assess whether your cybersecurity measures are effective, not just in place.
requirements.guidance: Define how effectiveness is measured, using indicators such as patch times, incidents and test results. Combine internal reviews, technical testing such as penetration tests and management reviews. Track findings to closure and report to leadership. Auditors find controls assumed to work and testing that is never followed up. Plan a testing calendar proportionate to your risk, over a period you set; many entities plan a year ahead.
questions: How do you measure whether controls are effective?
What testing has been done in the past year?
How are findings tracked and closed?
How do results reach management?

requirements.title: Basic cyber hygiene and training
requirements.purpose: Requires the everyday good practices, such as updates, strong passwords and backups, plus regular training to keep them working.
requirements.guidance: Write a short hygiene baseline for devices and accounts: updates, endpoint protection, least privilege, secure configuration and safe email and web use. Enforce through central management where possible rather than rely on goodwill. Back it with onboarding and refresher training. Auditors find laptops outside management, local admin rights for everyone and unmanaged personal devices. Measure compliance with the baseline.
questions: What is your baseline for devices and accounts?
How do you check devices meet it?
How are staff trained on safe working?
How do you handle exceptions?

requirements.title: Use of cryptography and encryption
requirements.purpose: Requires policies and procedures for when and how cryptography and encryption are used.
requirements.guidance: Write a short policy stating what must be encrypted in transit and at rest, approved algorithms and key management responsibilities. Cover devices, backups, email where needed and external connections. Manage certificates and keys with owners, expiry tracking and secure storage. Auditors find expired certificates, unencrypted laptops and keys kept in code repositories. Review the policy when standards change.
questions: What data and systems must be encrypted and where is this defined?
How are keys created, stored and rotated?
How do you track certificate expiry?
How do you check devices and backups are encrypted?

requirements.title: People security, access control and asset management
requirements.purpose: Requires controls for staff-related risk, who may access what, and knowing which assets you hold.
requirements.guidance: Screen staff proportionately, set security terms in contracts and run a joiner, mover, leaver process that grants and removes access promptly. Apply least privilege and review access at intervals you set; many entities review yearly, and privileged access more often. Keep an asset inventory of hardware, software, data and services with owners. Auditors find leavers with active accounts, inventories that are out of date and excessive admin rights. Automate where you can.
questions: How are access rights granted, changed and removed?
How often is access reviewed?
How do you keep the asset inventory current?
What checks are made before people start?
evidence: Joiner, mover, leaver procedure and tickets

requirements.title: Multi-factor sign-in and secured communications
requirements.purpose: Requires multi-factor or continuous authentication and secured voice, video, text and emergency communications, where appropriate to the risk.
requirements.guidance: Enable multi-factor authentication for remote access, admin accounts, email and critical applications, preferring phishing-resistant methods; continuous authentication is an accepted alternative. Use approved, encrypted communication tools and define a backup channel for emergencies if normal systems are down. Record where you decided strong authentication or secured channels are not appropriate, and why. Auditors find MFA gaps for service accounts and admins and no out-of-band contact plan. Keep exceptions time-limited with an owner.
questions: Where is multi-factor authentication enforced?
Which accounts are exempt and why?
What tools are approved for confidential communication?
How would you communicate if email were unavailable?

requirements.title: Considering each supplier's weaknesses and practices
requirements.purpose: Requires supplier security choices to reflect the particular weaknesses of each direct supplier, the quality of what it delivers and how securely it develops, and any EU-level supply chain risk findings.
requirements.guidance: Assess direct suppliers one by one rather than with a single standard, looking at their security posture, past incidents, how they build and maintain their products and how dependent you are on them. You must also take into account the results of EU coordinated risk assessments of critical supply chains, such as the one on 5G networks, where they cover your suppliers. Record the risk and the mitigations, such as limiting access or requiring certifications. Auditors find generic questionnaires with no follow-up on poor answers. Reassess at renewal or after supplier incidents.
questions: How do you assess an individual supplier's security practices and product quality?
How do you check a supplier's secure development practices?
What do you do when a supplier scores poorly?
Which EU coordinated supply chain risk assessments apply to your suppliers, and how did you act on them?
When are suppliers reassessed?

requirements.title: Fixing gaps in the measures without undue delay
requirements.purpose: Requires you to take corrective action promptly when you find that a measure does not meet the required standard.
requirements.guidance: Keep a corrective action register for every audit finding, test result and incident cause, with owner, priority and due date. Track to closure and report overdue items to management. Verify that fixes work. Auditors find long-open items and findings repeated year after year. Agree realistic timelines and escalate when they slip.
questions: How are gaps recorded and assigned?
How do you prioritise and time-box fixes?
What happens when an action is overdue?
How do you verify a fix?

requirements.title: Article 23 · Reporting obligations
requirements.purpose: Requires in-scope organisations to tell the authorities quickly about significant incidents, in stages.

requirements.title: Report significant incidents to the CSIRT or authority
requirements.purpose: Requires you to notify the national incident response team or competent authority of incidents with a significant impact on your services.
requirements.guidance: Identify which CSIRT or competent authority you report to, through which national entry point, and keep contact details and portal access ready. Name who decides to notify and who submits, with deputies. Fold the duty into your incident procedure with templates. Where a significant incident is likely to affect the services you provide, tell the recipients without undue delay; where they face a significant threat, tell them what they can do. A personal data breach also needs a separate GDPR assessment, and financial entities under DORA report under DORA instead. Auditors find organisations that do not know their reporting channel until an incident occurs.
questions: Which authority or CSIRT would you report to, and through which channel?
Who decides to notify and who submits?
How do you inform affected service recipients, and who approves the message?
How do you coordinate NIS2 reporting with GDPR breach notification or other sector rules?
Have you tested the reporting route?
evidence: Notification templates for the authority and for service recipients
Mapping of overlapping reporting duties such as GDPR and sector rules

requirements.title: What makes an incident significant
requirements.purpose: Defines when an incident must be reported: when it has caused or could cause severe disruption or financial loss to you, or considerable damage to other people or organisations.
requirements.guidance: Write practical criteria for significance covering service disruption, financial loss, number of people affected and material or non-material harm, aligned to national guidance. Remember that potential impact counts, not only actual damage. Digital providers covered by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 must use the thresholds it sets. Add a triage step so someone judges this early in every incident, and record the reasoning even when you decide not to report. Review the criteria when guidance changes. Auditors find vague thresholds and unrecorded decisions.
questions: What criteria do you use to judge an incident significant?
Who makes the judgement and by when?
Where is the decision recorded?
How do you keep the criteria aligned with national guidance?
evidence: Decision log for reported and unreported incidents

requirements.title: Early warning within 24 hours
requirements.purpose: Requires a first notice without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident, saying whether it may be malicious or have cross-border impact.
requirements.guidance: Prepare a short early warning template and a way to send it at any hour. The 24 hours is an outer limit, not a target. Do not wait for full facts: say what is known, whether unlawful or malicious action is suspected and whether other countries may be affected. Set an internal clock from the moment of awareness and record that moment. The CSIRT or authority should reply, where possible within 24 hours, and can offer support on request. Auditors find that nobody can submit outside office hours and that teams wait for certainty.
questions: How do you send an early warning at night or on weekends?
What does your early warning template include?
How do you record the time you became aware?
Who is the backup submitter?
evidence: Timeline of past or test notifications

requirements.title: Incident notification within 72 hours
requirements.purpose: Requires a fuller notification without undue delay and at the latest within 72 hours of becoming aware, updating the early warning with an initial assessment of severity and impact.
requirements.guidance: Prepare a template covering severity, impact, indicators of compromise where available and the updated assessment. Assign someone to gather facts from technical teams and review before submission. Update the earlier statement if the facts changed. Trust service providers have a shorter limit of 24 hours for incidents affecting their trust services. Auditors find notices that merely repeat the early warning or arrive late because approvals were not planned. Pre-agree who signs off.
questions: Who gathers the information for the 72-hour notification?
Who approves it before submission?
What does the template contain?
How do you correct the earlier warning?
evidence: Sample completed notification from an exercise

requirements.title: Intermediate report when asked
requirements.purpose: Requires status updates on request from the authority or CSIRT while the incident is still going on.
requirements.guidance: Make sure you can quickly produce a status summary: current state, actions taken, remaining risk and next steps. Keep a single incident log that can feed the report. Name the person who responds to authority requests. Auditors find teams unable to supply updates because information is scattered. Rehearse this in exercises.
questions: How would you respond to a request for an update mid-incident?
Who is the point of contact for the authority?
Where is the single source of incident information?
How do you keep reports consistent over time?

requirements.title: Final report within one month
requirements.purpose: Requires a detailed final report no later than one month after the 72-hour incident notification, covering severity, impact, likely root cause, mitigation and any cross-border effect.
requirements.guidance: Diary the final report as soon as the 72-hour notification goes in, with an owner and a due date one month later. Explain what happened and how serious it was, the threat or root cause that most likely triggered it, what you did and are still doing to contain it and whether other countries were affected. If the incident is still running at that point, send a progress report instead and the final report within one month of finishing handling the incident. Auditors find missed deadlines and shallow root cause analysis. Turn the lessons into corrective actions.
questions: Who owns the final report and how is the one-month deadline tracked?
How do you establish root cause?
What do you send if the incident is still ongoing at one month?
How are lessons turned into actions?
evidence: Deadline tracking in the incident log

requirements.title: Tell recipients about significant cyber threats and what they can do
requirements.purpose: Requires you to tell service recipients who may be affected by a significant cyber threat which measures or remedies they can take, and where appropriate about the threat itself.
requirements.guidance: A significant cyber threat is one whose technical features suggest it could severely affect your systems or your users through material or non-material damage (Article 6(11)). This duty applies before anything has happened, so treat it separately from incident reporting. Name who judges whether a threat is significant and which recipients may be affected, and keep customer contact lists current per service. Prepare short message templates that say what recipients can do themselves, such as installing an update, changing a setting or watching for a phishing campaign, and decide when to describe the threat too. Where telling people could help attackers, agree timing with your CSIRT. Keep a record of each threat assessed, who was told and when. Auditors find customer notices sent only after incidents, never for threats, and nobody owning the decision.
questions: Who decides whether a cyber threat is significant and which service recipients may be affected?
How do you reach affected recipients quickly, and how current are the contact lists?
Which measures or remedies have you recently told recipients about, and why?
When do you also describe the threat itself, and who approves that wording?
How do threat notices link to your incident process and to the CSIRT?
evidence: Procedure for assessing significant cyber threats and informing recipients
Message templates for recipients with measures and remedies
Log of threats assessed, recipients told and dates
Copies of notices sent to recipients

requirements.title: Article 2 · Scope
requirements.purpose: Sets out which organisations the directive covers: mainly medium-sized and larger entities in the sectors of Annexes I and II, plus some that are covered whatever their size.

requirements.title: Medium-sized and larger entities in the sectors of Annexes I and II
requirements.purpose: Brings into scope public and private entities of a type listed in Annex I or II that are at least medium-sized and provide their services or carry out their activities in the EU.
requirements.guidance: Treat this as a guided self-check and record the outcome. Step 1: list your services and activities and compare them with the sectors, subsectors and entity types in Annex I (such as energy, transport, banking, health, drinking water, digital infrastructure, ICT service management and public administration) and Annex II (such as postal services, waste, chemicals, food, manufacturing, digital providers and research). Step 2: apply the size-cap rule. Using Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC, you are in scope if you have at least 50 staff, or both annual turnover and balance sheet total above EUR 10 million. Count partner and linked enterprises as the Recommendation requires, and check whether national guidance adjusts this for groups. Step 3: confirm you provide services or carry out activities in the EU. If step 1 or 2 says no, check Article 2(2) before concluding you are out of scope. Auditors find scoping decided by size alone, with no sector mapping on file.
questions: Which of your services or activities match a sector, subsector or entity type in Annex I or II?
What are your headcount, annual turnover and balance sheet total, and how did you count partner and linked enterprises?
In which Member States do you provide services or carry out activities?
Who signed off the scoping decision, and what would make you recheck it?
Which national transposing law did you check, and does it widen the sectors or the size rule?
evidence: Scoping self-check mapping services to the sectors and entity types in Annexes I and II
Headcount, turnover and balance sheet figures used, with the year and source
Group structure showing partner and linked enterprises
List of Member States where services are provided
Management sign-off of the scoping decision
Note on the national transposing law consulted

requirements.title: Entities in scope regardless of size
requirements.purpose: Brings some entities into scope whatever their size, because of the service they provide or how critical they are, so a small entity cannot assume it is out of scope.
requirements.guidance: Check each of these even if the size-cap rule leaves you out. In scope regardless of size: providers of public electronic communications networks or publicly available electronic communications services; trust service providers; top-level domain name registries and DNS service providers; and central government bodies (and regional ones where national law says so). A Member State can also bring in an Annex I or II entity that is the sole national provider of a service essential for critical societal or economic activities, whose disruption could significantly affect public safety, security or health or cause significant systemic risk, or that is critical for its specific national or regional importance. Entities designated critical under Directive (EU) 2022/2557 (CER) are covered too, and domain name registration services are covered for the registration data duties in Article 28. National law may add local government or education. Public bodies working mainly in national security, defence or law enforcement are excluded. Auditors find small providers that assumed they were out of scope.
questions: Do you provide a public electronic communications network or service, a trust service, a TLD name registry or a DNS service?
Has the authority identified you as a sole national provider, or as critical for public safety, security, health or systemic risk?
Have you been designated a critical entity under the CER Directive?
Does your national law bring in further entity types, such as local government or education?
evidence: Checklist of the size-independent criteria with the answer and reason for each
Any letter or decision from the authority identifying the entity
CER designation, where there is one
Note on national additions to scope

requirements.title: Article 3 · Essential and important entities
requirements.purpose: Sorts in-scope entities into essential and important, which decides how closely they are supervised and the maximum fines, and requires each Member State to keep a list of them.

requirements.title: Essential entities
requirements.purpose: Defines which in-scope entities are essential: mainly large entities in Annex I sectors, plus certain providers and bodies named whatever their size or identified by the Member State.
requirements.guidance: Continue the self-check from Article 2. You are essential if you are: an Annex I entity above the medium-sized ceilings (250 or more staff, or turnover above EUR 50 million and balance sheet total above EUR 43 million); a qualified trust service provider, TLD name registry or DNS service provider, whatever your size; a medium-sized provider of public electronic communications networks or services; an in-scope central government body; an entity the Member State identifies as essential under Article 2(2)(b) to (e); an entity designated critical under the CER Directive; or, where the Member State so decides, an operator of essential services under the first NIS Directive. Essential entities are supervised proactively, including audits, inspections and security scans, and face national maximum fines of at least EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Record the criterion you applied, the reasoning and the date.
questions: Which criterion makes you essential, or why does none apply?
Do your figures exceed the medium-sized ceilings, counted as the Recommendation requires?
Has the Member State identified you as essential, now or under the first NIS Directive?
How are you prepared for proactive supervision, such as audits or on-site inspections by the authority?
evidence: Classification record naming the criterion applied
Size figures and the group calculation used
Any identification decision from the authority
Plan for supporting supervisory audits and inspections

requirements.title: Important entities
requirements.purpose: Makes every other in-scope entity of a type in Annex I or II an important entity, including those a Member State identifies as important.
requirements.guidance: If you are in scope under Article 2 but meet none of the essential criteria, you are important. Typical cases are medium-sized entities in Annex I sectors and medium-sized or large entities in Annex II sectors, such as manufacturers, food businesses or digital providers. The risk-management measures in Article 21 and the reporting duties in Article 23 are the same as for essential entities. What differs is supervision, which happens after the event when there are signs of non-compliance, and the national maximum fines of at least EUR 7 million or 1.4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Your class can change when you grow, shrink, merge or start a new service, so recheck it on those events and at intervals you set; many entities review yearly. Financial entities covered by DORA follow DORA for risk management and incident reporting; check how your national law treats them for classification and registration.
questions: On what basis did you conclude that you are an important rather than an essential entity?
Which events would change your class, and who watches for them?
How do you show you meet Articles 21 and 23 when supervision only follows signs of non-compliance?
Does a sector-specific law such as DORA replace parts of NIS2 for you?
evidence: List of events that trigger a reclassification, such as growth, mergers or new services
Record of the latest classification review
Note on overlapping sector-specific law, where relevant

requirements.title: National list of entities and the information you submit
requirements.purpose: Requires each Member State to keep a list of essential and important entities, and requires entities to give the authority their details and to report changes within two weeks.
requirements.guidance: Member States had to establish the list by 17 April 2025 and must review it at least every two years. In most countries the authority will not tell you that you are in scope: you are expected to make the determination yourself and register, often through a national portal. Submit at least your name, address and current contact details including email addresses, IP ranges and telephone numbers, your sector and subsector under Annex I or II, and where applicable the Member States where you provide in-scope services. Report any change to these details without delay and in any event within two weeks. National law sets the deadline for first registration and may ask for more, such as a security contact. Digital providers listed in Article 27 also have the duties in that article. Auditors find entities that are in scope but never registered, and stale contact details.
questions: Have you registered with the competent authority, through which channel, and when?
What information did you submit, and who keeps it current?
How would a change of address, contact details or IP ranges reach the authority within two weeks?
What deadline and extra information does your national law set for registration?
evidence: Self-determination record that led to registration
Registration confirmation from the competent authority
Owner and procedure for notifying changes within two weeks

requirements.title: Article 27 · Registry of entities
requirements.purpose: Requires certain digital infrastructure and digital service providers to give their details to one authority, so that ENISA can keep an EU-wide registry of them.

requirements.title: Registration of digital providers with the authority
requirements.purpose: Requires DNS, TLD, domain registration, cloud, data centre, CDN, managed and managed security service providers, online marketplaces, search engines and social networks to register their details and keep them current.
requirements.guidance: First check whether you are one of these entity types. If so, register with the competent authority of the Member State of your main establishment in the EU (Article 26), or of your representative if you are established outside the EU. The directive's deadline was 17 January 2025. Submit your name; your sector, subsector and entity type under Annex I or II; the address of your main establishment and your other establishments in the EU, or of your representative; current contact details including email addresses and telephone numbers; the Member States where you provide services; and your IP ranges. Report changes without delay and in any event within three months. The authority passes the details to ENISA. National transposition sets the channel and may add fields or extend registration to other entities, so read your national law. Auditors find registrations made once and never updated after an office move or a new IP range.
questions: Which entity type in Article 27 applies to you, and in which Member State is your main establishment?
When did you register, and with which authority?
Who keeps the registered details current, and how are changes reported within three months?
Are your registered IP ranges and contact details correct today?
What does your national law add to the registration duty?
evidence: Registration confirmation from the competent authority
Copy of the submitted details, including IP ranges
Determination of the main establishment or representative
Change log with the dates changes were notified
Owner and procedure for keeping the registration current
